stem: What is the primary purpose of the United States Twenty-First Century Communications and Video Accessibility Act (CVAA)?

options.text: To ensure that modern mobile, broadband, and internet-streamed video programming technologies are accessible to individuals with disabilities.
options.shortLabel: Accessible broadband, mobile, and IP video
options.rationale: Enacted in 2010, the CVAA updated federal communications law to mandate that advanced communications services (including VoIP, video conferencing, and mobile browsers) and IP-delivered video are accessible to people with disabilities.

options.text: To mandate that federal government agencies procure and maintain accessible electronic information technologies and public digital documentation.
options.rationale: The procurement, development, and maintenance of accessible information and communication technology by federal agencies is governed by Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act, not the CVAA.

options.text: To establish compulsory technical accessibility standards for private commercial e-commerce websites and online retail storefronts.
options.rationale: Accessibility for private commercial websites and online public accommodations falls under Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), rather than FCC telecommunications rules under the CVAA.

options.text: To govern traditional analog broadcast television captioning and wireline telephone equipment across state telecommunications utilities.
options.rationale: Legacy wireline telecommunications and broadcast TV closed captioning were established under Section 255 and the Telecommunications Act of 1996; the CVAA was created specifically to bridge the gap into 21st-century digital, mobile, and IP technologies.

explanation: Enacted in 2010, the Twenty-First Century Communications and Video Accessibility Act (CVAA) modernized US communications law under the Federal Communications Commission (FCC). It closed the regulatory gap between legacy telecommunications and modern digital media by requiring that Advanced Communications Services (ACS)—such as interconnected VoIP, video conferencing, text messaging, and mobile web browsers—as well as video programming delivered via the internet (IP-streamed video that previously aired on TV) are fully accessible to individuals with disabilities.
